idiom_name: ERB template with <% %> / <%= %> rendered by ActionView
implementation_notes: ERB ships in the Ruby standard library, so the scriptlet form is part of the platform: <% %> runs Ruby without emitting output, <%= %> writes the expression's value, and Rails' ActionView handler is ERB applied to .html.erb views, with helpers and partials as the framework's answer to logic in the view. Escaping is not ERB's own default - Rails' html_safe? protocol and raw decide what is escaped - so the classic structure is justified for small pages and scripts, while a Rails view that queries or mutates state is the pattern's failure mode: the framework already provides the controller half.
code_sketch:
<%# app/views/users/index.html.erb - ActionView renders this per request %>
    <% @users.each do |u| %>
  • <%= u.name %> (<%= u.logins %>)
    • <% end %>
pitfalls: <%= %> interpolates without escaping in plain ERB; Rails escapes by default, but raw, html_safe and string-built content_tag arguments switch that protection off.

Rendering ERB through the controller (render inline:, or ERB.new(...).result) embeds the page in the request path and defeats MVC - the Rails guide calls it horrid coding practice and for good reason.
An ERB template evaluates in a binding, so it reaches any local in scope: a view can mutate controller state or trigger lazy ActiveRecord loads, turning one render into N queries.
Template errors surface while the response is already being written, producing a half-rendered page or a double-render error instead of a clean failure.
